questions: how did early internet researchers coordinate
subtitle: Announcement of a 1970 network protocol meeting at UCLA

tldr.problem: The early ARPANET researchers needed to coordinate on protocol details and gather feedback from different sites.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 35 is a meeting announcement for a live presentation of the network protocol at UCLA on March 17, 1970, with coordination details and a contact number for arrangements.
tldr.outcome: This is a historical record of how early ARPANET researchers coordinated, demonstrating the collaborative process that shaped modern networking.

today: RFC 35 is a historical record of how early ARPANET researchers coordinated their efforts. It is not obsolete but rather a documentation of early Internet history.

sections.title: The Meeting Announcement
sections.content:
RFC 35 is a memo from Stephen Crocker of UCLA announcing a live network meeting to discuss protocol details. The meeting was scheduled for Tuesday, March 17, 1970 at 9:00 a.m. at UCLA. This was an early coordination mechanism for ARPANET researchers.

The announcement indicates that detailed protocol documentation from NWG/RFC #33 would be ready for presentation. The meeting was intended to be a forum for feedback and discussion before the protocol was finalized.
sections.plainLanguage: In 1970, computer scientists had to announce meetings the old-fashioned way. This RFC says: we're meeting at UCLA on this date to talk about how the network will work.

sections.title: Participation and Next Steps
sections.content:
To keep the meeting productive, the announcement requested that each site send only one programmer. The announcement also suggested leaving March 18 open in case discussions ran longer.

The plan was for documentation to be presented at the meeting, and if no major flaws were discovered, it would be released as an RFC on March 20. Attendees needing help with travel or lodging could contact Mrs. Charlotte LaRoche at the UCLA number listed.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule was one programmer per organization so everyone could actually talk. If the meeting went well, the final network rules would be sent out by the weekend.

sections.title: Early ARPANET Collaboration
sections.content:
RFC 35 is a historical document showing how early computer scientists coordinated to develop the ARPANET. Before email, video conferencing, or instant messaging, organizing a meeting required sending out an RFC with phone numbers and physical addresses.

The focus on protocol standardization and the need for live discussion underscores how collaborative the early networking effort was. Each site had to send someone who could understand and debate technical details, suggesting the network was still small enough for that to be feasible.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo shows how scientists met face-to-face to decide how computers would talk to each other, using phone calls to arrange travel and meetings.
